subject: math
title: Grade 4 Money and Financial Literacy: Ways to Pay, Total Cost and Making Change
seo_title: Grade 4 Money Worksheets: Making Change, Total Cost and Ways to Pay (Free, Answer Key, Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Estimate and calculate the cost of transactions involving multiple items priced in whole-dollar amounts, not including sales tax, and the amount of change needed when payment is made in cash, using mental math
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 money and financial literacy math worksheets for the Ontario curriculum: cash, debit, credit and gift cards, the total cost of several items in whole dollars, making change from $20, $50 and $100 by counting up, spending, saving and donating, and finding the better buy. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: To find change, count up from the price to the money paid: $37 → $40 → $50 is $3 + $10 = $13.
key_sub: Add prices in your head by making tens ($8 + $12 = $20) and using friendly numbers ($19 = $20 − $1). Debit spends your own money; credit is borrowed and must be paid back.
body_html:
Ways to pay

There is more than one way to pay. Each one works in a different way.

Way to payHow it worksGood to know
CashCoins and bills you hand overYou can see what is left. You may get change. Does not work online
Debit cardTakes money straight from your bank accountExact amount. You can only spend what is in the account
Credit cardBorrows money you pay back when the bill comesEasy to overspend. Extra fees (interest) if paid late
Gift cardHas a set amount on it, often a presentUsually works only at one store. The amount goes down each time

Total cost: add the prices in your head

Look for prices that make a ten. Use a friendly number: $19 is $20 − $1.

Example

Find the total of $19 and $24.

$20 + $24 = $44. Take back the $1: $44 − $1 = $43.

Answer: $43

To estimate, round each price to the nearest $10 first: $38 + $61 is about $40 + $60 = $100.

Change: count up from the price

Start at the price. Jump to the next $10. Then jump to the money paid. Add the jumps.

Example

A book costs $37. You pay with a $50 bill. What is the change?

$37 + $3 = $40. $40 + $10 = $50. $3 + $10 = $13. Check: $37 + $13 = $50.

Answer: $13

Spend, save, donate

Earning is getting money for work. Spending is buying things. Saving is keeping money for later. Investing is putting money where it can grow, like a bank account that pays interest. Donating is giving money to help others.

Is it a good buy?

Compare the cost of the same amount. 3 notebooks at $3 each cost $9, so a pack of 3 for $6 is the better buy. A bigger pack is not always cheaper, so check. And something you do not need is never a good buy.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding to find change: $37 + $50 = $87Change is less than the money paid. Count up from $37 to $50: $13
Counting up wrongly: $37 to $50 is $3 + $20Jump to the next ten ($40), then only $10 more to $50
Forgetting one item in the totalTick off each price as you add it
$26 + $15 = $316 + 5 = 11 ones. Regroup 10 ones as a ten: $41
Buying the bigger pack without checkingFind the cost of the same number of things first

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about money in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario Grade 4 financial literacy strand, students learn different ways to pay, add the cost of several items priced in whole dollars, find the change from a cash payment using mental math, and talk about spending, saving, earning, investing and donating.

faq.q: How do you teach making change in Grade 4?
faq.a: Count up from the price to the money paid. For a $37 item paid with $50, jump $3 to $40, then $10 to $50, so the change is $13. Then check that the price plus the change equals the money paid.

faq.q: What is the difference between a debit card and a credit card for kids?
faq.a: A debit card takes the money straight from your own bank account. A credit card borrows the money, and you must pay the bill later, with extra fees if you pay late.

faq.q: Is sales tax included in Grade 4 money questions?
faq.a: No. The Grade 4 expectation uses whole-dollar prices without sales tax. Ontario’s 13% HST is added to money problems in Grade 6.

sets.title: Ways to pay: cash, debit, credit and gift cards

items.q: Which of these is cash?
items.e: Cash is money you can hold: coins (nickels, dimes, quarters, loonies, toonies) and bills.

items.q: Which way to pay takes the money straight out of your own bank account?
items.e: A debit card takes the money right away from your bank account. You can only spend money that is in the account.

items.q: Which way to pay means you borrow the money now and pay a bill later?
items.e: With a credit card, the card company pays the store. You get a bill later and must pay it back.

items.q: Which way to pay has a set amount of money on it and is often given as a present?
items.e: A gift card is loaded with a set amount, such as $25. Each time you buy something, that amount goes down.

items.q: Which way to pay is the only one you can hand to a friend at a lemonade stand that has no card machine?
items.e: A card needs a card machine or a website. Cash can be paid anywhere, even at a lemonade stand.

items.q: Which way to pay cannot be used to buy something from an online store?
items.e: You cannot hand coins and bills over the internet. Online stores need a card, so cash does not work.

items.q: Nathan gets a gift card for a bookstore. Where can he use it?
c: At a bank, to get cash
items.e: Most gift cards work only at the store that sold them, so he can use it at that bookstore.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a way to pay?
items.e: A library card lets you borrow books for free. It has no money on it, so you cannot pay with it.

items.q: You pay for a $13 book with a debit card. What happens?
c: You get a bill to pay later
items.e: Debit takes the exact price, $13, from your bank account. There is no change, because no cash was handed over.

items.q: Ethan’s grandma pays for a $60 bike helmet with her credit card. Is the helmet free?
c: Yes, the card pays for it
No, the store pays for it
No, she pays the bill later
Yes, if she keeps the receipt
items.e: A credit card borrows the money. Grandma gets a bill and must pay the $60 back, so it is not free.

items.q: What is one risk of using a credit card?
c: Spending more than you can pay back
It runs out after one use
It only works at one store
items.e: It is easy to buy lots of things and forget it is borrowed money. If you spend more than you can pay back, you owe money and extra fees.

items.q: What is one good reason to pay with cash?
c: You can see how much you have left
items.e: With cash in your wallet, you can see how much is left, so it is hard to overspend. But cash can be lost, and it does not work online.

items.q: Lucas’s debit card is linked to a bank account with $40 in it. Can he buy a $55 jacket with only that card?
items.e: Debit can only spend what is in the account. $55 − $40 = $15, so he is $15 short. ($95 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Ava pays for a $7 lunch with a $10 bill. Does she get change?
items.e: Cash paid is more than the price, so there is change. Count up: $7 + $3 = $10. $3 change. ($17 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Owen buys a $9 puzzle with this gift card. How much is left on the card?
items.e: Count up from $9 to $25: $9 + $1 = $10, $10 + $15 = $25. $1 + $15 = $16 is left. ($34 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Jayden has this gift card. He wants a $36 hockey stick. What can he do?
items.e: The card covers $30. $36 − $30 = $6, so he must pay $6 more with cash or a debit card.

items.q: Chloe has a $20 gift card for a toy store and $5 in cash. She buys a $23 game. How much cash does she use?
items.e: The gift card pays $20 first. $23 − $20 = $3 is paid in cash. ($43 adds the card and the price.)

items.q: A family spends $200 at the grocery store. Why might they pay with debit instead of cash?
c: They do not need to carry lots of bills
items.e: Paying $200 in cash means carrying many bills, which could be lost. With debit, they do not need to carry the bills. The price is the same either way.

items.q: Which way to pay can lead to extra fees, called interest, if the bill is not paid on time?
items.e: A credit card is borrowed money. If you do not pay the bill on time, the card company adds interest, so you pay back more than you spent.

items.q: Sofia taps her phone to pay. The phone is linked to her debit card. Where does the money come from?
c: A loan to pay back later
items.e: The phone works like the debit card it is linked to, so the money comes from her bank account.

items.q: What is the total for the ball and the pump?
items.e: $8 + $6: make a ten. $8 + $2 = $10, then $4 more. Total: $14.

items.q: What is the total for the paint set and the brushes?
What do the mitts and the hat cost together?
items.e: Add the tens: $10 + $10 = $20. Add the ones: $5 + $3 = $8. Total: $28.

items.q: Hana buys a $26 book and a $15 calendar. What is the total cost?
Mateo buys a $19 lunch box and a $24 water bottle. What is the total?
items.e: $19 is $1 less than $20. $20 + $24 = $44, then take away the $1: $43. ($44 forgets to take the $1 back.)

items.q: Kai buys the pencils, the eraser and the ruler. What is the total?
items.e: $4 + $2 + $3 = $9. Check that all three prices are added.

items.q: Priya buys 3 skipping ropes at $7 each. What is the total cost?
items.e: 3 × $7 = $21. Or add: $7 + $7 + $7 = $21. ($10 adds 3 + 7 instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Arjun buys a $35 sweater and a $48 pair of jeans. What is the total cost?
items.e: $35 + $48: $35 + $50 = $85, then take away $2: $83. ($73 forgets to regroup 13 ones as 1 ten.)

items.q: What is the total for all three items?
items.e: Add numbers that make a ten first: $8 + $12 = $20. Then $20 + $5 = $25.

items.q: Mei buys 4 tickets to a hockey game at $9 each. What is the total cost?
Olivia buys 2 T-shirts at $14 each and a cap for $9. What is the total?
items.e: T-shirts: 2 × $14 = $28. Add the cap: $28 + $9 = $37. ($23 counts only one T-shirt.)

items.q: A family buys the tent and the lantern for a canoe trip. What is the total?
items.e: $89 is $1 less than $90. $90 + $23 = $113, then take away $1: $112. ($102 forgets to regroup.)

items.q: At the school book fair, Emma buys books for $6, $11 and $14. What is the total?
Benjamin buys a $125 bike and a $38 helmet. What is the total cost?
About how much do the boots and the jacket cost together? Round each price to the nearest $10.
items.e: $38 rounds to $40. $61 rounds to $60. $40 + $60 = about $100. ($99 is the exact total, not the estimate.)

items.q: Aiden has $60. He wants items that cost $22, $29 and $18. Round to the nearest $10 to estimate. Is $60 enough?
For a class party, Maya’s teacher buys juice for $17, fruit for $23 and cups for $8. What is the total?
items.e: $17 + $23 = $40 (7 + 3 makes a ten). $40 + $8 = $48. ($38 forgets to regroup the ten.)

items.q: Amira buys 5 packs of hockey cards at $12 a pack. What is the total cost?
A family buys the skates, the helmet and the stick. What is the total?
Zoe buys 2 movie tickets at $18 each and 2 drinks at $7 each. What is the total?
items.e: Tickets: 2 × $18 = $36. Drinks: 2 × $7 = $14. $36 + $14 = $50. ($25 counts only one ticket and one drink.)

sets.title: Change from $20, $50 and $100 by counting up

items.q: Leah buys a $7 book and pays with a $10 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from $7 to $10: $7 + $3 = $10. The change is $3.

items.q: Liam buys a $16 puzzle and pays with a $20 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $16 to $20: $16 + $4 = $20. The change is $4. Check: $16 + $4 = $20.

items.q: Use the number line. A toy costs $12. You pay with a $20 bill. How much change do you get?
items.e: Count up from $12 to $20: $12 + $8 = $20. The change is $8.

items.q: Noah buys a $9 kite and pays with a $20 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $9 to $20: $9 + $1 = $10, then $10 + $10 = $20. Add the jumps: $1 + $10 = $11. ($29 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Nathan buys a $13 book about loons and pays with a $20 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $13 to $20: $13 + $7 = $20. The change is $7.

items.q: Use the number line. Shin pads cost $34. You pay with a $50 bill. How much change do you get?
Ethan buys a $37 sweater and pays with a $50 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $37 to $50: $37 + $3 = $40, then $40 + $10 = $50. Add the jumps: $3 + $10 = $13. ($27 comes from 7 − 0 = 7 and 5 − 3 = 2: you cannot take 7 from 0, so regroup or count up.)

items.q: Lucas buys a $26 board game and pays with a $50 bill. How much change does he get?
Ava buys a $41 soccer ball and pays with a $50 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from $41 to $50: $41 + $9 = $50. The change is $9.

items.q: Owen buys an $18 pair of mitts and pays with a $50 bill. How much change does he get?
Use the number line. A hockey jersey costs $62. You pay with a $100 bill. How much change do you get?
Jayden buys a $45 backpack and pays with a $100 bill. How much change does he get?
Chloe buys a $78 pair of skates and pays with a $100 bill. How much change does she get?
Sofia pays for a $43 jacket with these bills. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from $43 to $50: $43 + $7 = $50. The change is $7. The bills make $20 + $20 + $10 = $50.

items.q: Hana pays for an $87 tent with these bills. How much change does she get?
Which shows the right way to count up from $37 to $50?
items.e: $37 + $3 = $40 (the next ten). $40 + $10 = $50. So $3 + $10 = $13. ($7 is how far $37 is from $30, the wrong way.)

items.q: Mateo pays with a $50 bill and gets $14 in change. What was the price?
items.e: Price + change = money paid. $50 − $14: count up from $14 to $50. $14 + $6 = $20, $20 + $30 = $50, so $36. Check: $36 + $14 = $50. The price was $36. ($64 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Kai buys a $12 book and a $5 bookmark. He pays with a $20 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Total: $12 + $5 = $17. Count up from $17 to $20: $3. ($8 forgets the bookmark; $15 forgets the book.)

items.q: Priya buys a $24 ball and a $19 pump. She pays with a $50 bill. How much change does she get?
Arjun buys 3 books at $15 each and a $28 lamp. He pays with a $100 bill. How much change does he get?
What does earning money mean?
c: Putting money in a piggy bank
Getting paid for work you do
items.e: Earning is getting money for work, like raking leaves or shovelling snow. The others are saving, donating and spending.

items.q: Which is an example of donating?
items.e: Donating means giving money to help others, like a food bank or the Terry Fox Run.

items.q: Which is an example of saving?
c: Keeping $10 to buy a bike later
items.e: Saving is keeping money now so you can use it later, like for a bike.

items.q: Which is an example of investing?
c: Putting money where it can grow
items.e: Investing is putting money in a place where it can grow over time, like a bank account that pays interest. Money under a bed does not grow.

items.q: Which is a need, not a want?
items.e: A need is something you must have to be safe and healthy. In a Canadian winter, warm boots are a need. The others are wants.

items.q: If Mei spends more of her allowance each week, what happens to her savings?
items.e: Spending and saving come from the same money. If Mei spends more, there is less left, so she saves less.

items.q: Before buying something, which is the best question to ask?
c: Is the box a nice colour?
Do I need it or want it?
items.e: Asking “Do I need it or want it?” helps you decide if it is worth the money.

items.q: Olivia earned $30. She puts $12 in the Spend jar and $3 in the Donate jar. The rest goes in the Save jar. How much is saved?
items.e: Spend and donate: $12 + $3 = $15. Save: $30 − $15 = $15. ($45 adds everything instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Emma earns $5 each week for doing chores. How much does she earn in 6 weeks?
Benjamin rakes leaves for 4 neighbours. Each one pays $6. How much does he earn?
Aiden gets $20 for his birthday. He saves half and donates $2. How much can he spend?
items.e: Half of $20 is $10 saved. $20 − $10 = $10 left. Donate $2: $10 − $2 = $8 to spend. ($10 forgets the donation.)

items.q: Maya saves $4 each week. How many weeks will it take to save $28?
items.e: Count by 4s to 28: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. That is 7 jumps, so 7 weeks. (28 ÷ 4 = 7. 24 weeks comes from $28 − $4.)

items.q: Amira has $15 saved. She wants a $45 skateboard and saves $5 each week. How many more weeks until she can buy it?
items.e: Still needed: $45 − $15 = $30. $30 ÷ $5 = 6 weeks. (9 weeks forgets the $15 already saved.)

items.q: Zoe puts $100 in a savings account. After a year, the bank adds $2 interest. How much is in the account now?
items.e: Interest is money the bank adds to your savings. $100 + $2 = $102. This is how saving in a bank helps money grow.

items.q: A Grade 4 class raises $86 at a bake sale and $47 at a car wash. They donate it all to the food bank. How much do they donate?
items.e: $86 + $47: $86 + $40 = $126, then $126 + $7 = $133. ($123 forgets to regroup the 13 ones; $39 subtracts.)

items.q: Leah has $50. She spends $18 on a hockey puck set and $12 on tape. How much is left to save?
items.e: Spent: $18 + $12 = $30. Left: $50 − $30 = $20. ($32 takes away only the $18; $80 adds.)

items.q: Both Liam and Noah get $10 a week. Liam saves $6 a week. Noah saves $2 a week. After 5 weeks, how much more has Liam saved?
items.e: Liam: 5 × $6 = $30. Noah: 5 × $2 = $10. $30 − $10 = $20 more. People make different choices: Noah spends more each week, Liam saves more. ($4 is the difference for only one week.)

items.q: Nathan splits his money into these jars. How much money did he split?
items.e: Add the jars: $9 + $15 + $6 = $30. Make a ten first: $9 + $6 = $15, $15 + $15 = $30. ($24 forgets the $6.)

items.q: Ethan earns $12 each week walking a neighbour’s dog. He saves $8 and spends the rest. How much does he spend in 4 weeks?
items.e: Spent each week: $12 − $8 = $4. In 4 weeks: 4 × $4 = $16. ($32 is the money saved: 4 × $8.)

items.q: Lucas wants to donate $40 to the Terry Fox Run. He has $25. He earns $5 for each driveway he shovels. How many driveways must he shovel?
items.e: Still needed: $40 − $25 = $15. $15 ÷ $5 = 3 driveways. (8 driveways forgets the $25 he already has.)

sets.title: Good buys and money word problems

items.q: You need 3 notebooks. Which is the better buy?
items.e: 3 single notebooks: 3 × $3 = $9. The pack: $6. $6 is less than $9, so the pack of 3 is the better buy.

items.q: How much do you save by buying the 6-pack instead of 6 single juice boxes?
Which maple syrup is the better buy?
items.e: Two 250 mL bottles make 500 mL and cost 2 × $8 = $16. The 500 mL bottle is $14. The 500 mL bottle is the better buy.

items.q: A $10 soccer ball breaks every 2 months. A $20 ball lasts all year. Which is the better value for one year?
items.e: In a year you would need 6 of the $10 balls: 6 × $10 = $60. One $20 ball lasts the year. The $20 ball is better value, even though its price is higher.

items.q: A shirt is on sale for $5, but you do not need it and will not wear it. Is it a good buy?
items.e: A good buy is something you need or will use at a fair price. If you will not wear it, the $5 is wasted.

items.q: Store A sells a ball for $24. Store B sells the same ball for $30 with $5 off. Which store is cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Store B: $30 − $5 = $25. Store A: $24. $25 − $24 = $1, so Store A is cheaper by $1. (Store A, by $6 forgets the $5 off.)

items.q: Public skating costs $5 a visit, or $40 for a 10-visit pass. For 10 visits, which is cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: 10 visits at $5: 10 × $5 = $50. The pass: $40. $50 − $40 = $10, so the pass is cheaper by $10. ($35 is $40 − $5.)

items.q: Ava has $40. She wants skates for $28 and a helmet for $15. Does she have enough?
items.e: Total: $28 + $15 = $43. $43 is more than $40. $43 − $40 = $3, so she is $3 short. ($12 left counts only the skates.)

items.q: Owen buys 4 tickets to the science centre at $12 each. He pays with a $50 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Tickets: 4 × $12 = $48. Count up from $48 to $50: $2. ($38 counts only one ticket.)

items.q: Jayden’s family goes to a movie. 3 tickets cost $11 each, and popcorn is $6. What is the total?
items.e: Tickets: 3 × $11 = $33. Add the popcorn: $33 + $6 = $39. ($33 forgets the popcorn.)

items.q: On a snow day, Chloe shovels 3 driveways at $15 each. She spends $18 on new mitts. How much money is left?
items.e: Earned: 3 × $15 = $45. Left: $45 − $18. Count up from $18: $2 to $20, then $25 to $45, so $27. ($63 adds the mitts.)

items.q: At the hardware store, Sofia buys a birdhouse kit for $22 and paint for $9. She pays with a $50 bill. How much change does she get?
Hana plans a picnic at the lake. Sandwiches cost $16, fruit costs $23 and drinks cost $9. Round to the nearest $10. About how much is the picnic?
Mateo buys 2 scarves and 1 pair of mitts. What is the total?
items.e: Scarves: 2 × $12 = $24. Add the mitts: $24 + $8 = $32. ($20 counts only one scarf.)

items.q: Kai has $25 on a gift card for a bookstore. He buys a $14 book and a $7 journal. How much is left on the card?
items.e: Total: $14 + $7 = $21. Left: count up from $21 to $25: $4. ($11 forgets the journal.)

items.q: Priya has $30. A pack of hockey cards costs $6. She buys 3 packs. How much money is left?
items.e: 3 packs: 3 × $6 = $18. Left: $30 − $18 = $12. ($24 takes away only one pack.)

items.q: A teacher needs 20 pencils. Which choice costs less?
items.e: Two boxes of 10: 2 × $4 = $8. One box of 20: $9. $8 is less, so two boxes of 10 cost less. A bigger box is not always the better buy.

items.q: Arjun has $60 saved. He spends $2 a week on snacks for 7 weeks. How much is left?
items.e: Snacks: 7 × $2 = $14. Left: $60 − $14 = $46. ($58 takes away only one week; $53 takes away $7.)

items.q: A Grade 4 class buys 5 board games at $8 each and a $15 puzzle for indoor recess. They pay with a $100 bill. How much change do they get?
items.e: Games: 5 × $8 = $40. Total: $40 + $15 = $55. Count up from $55: $5 to $60, $40 to $100. $5 + $40 = $45. ($77 counts only one game; $55 is the total, not the change.)

items.q: Mei’s family buys 2 canoe paddles at $35 each and an $18 life jacket for the cottage. They pay with a $100 bill. How much change do they get?
items.e: Paddles: 2 × $35 = $70. Total: $70 + $18 = $88. Count up: $88 + $2 = $90, $90 + $10 = $100. $2 + $10 = $12. ($47 counts only one paddle; $22 adds one $10 jump too many.)
